source.title: Not All Explanations for Deep Learning Phenomena Are Equally Valuable
source.authors: Alan Jeffares; M. van der Schaar

record.tranche_reason: The paper includes its own illustrative model-size example of double descent, using a setting from Greydanus and Kobak (2024), but it does not report a direct reproduction of the original studies' methods.
record.gate_note: Figure 4 and Appendix A report the paper's own example in which prime counts track test performance in a double-descent setting. The paper's schematic Figure 1 and its statements about regularization, scaling analyses, and parameter counting draw on prior work and are not additional rows.
record.test_reason: This is a position paper. Its only own experiment (Figure 4, left) re-runs a known double-descent setting from Greydanus & Kobak (2024, MNIST-1D). It runs the setting as a demonstration bed for a deliberately absurd 'prime-valued parameters' explanation. What it reports is how well prime counts track test performance, not whether double descent holds or where its peak falls. The paper's arguments that double descent is practically irrelevant, vanishes under regularization, and depends on parameter counting all rest on cited work (Nakkiran et al. 2021, Hastie et al. 2022, Curth et al. 2024b, Kaplan et al. 2020). None of them are its own results. So it relies on the phenomenon as a tool rather than testing any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors argue that double descent, like grokking and lottery tickets, is an edge case rarely seen in practice. Citing prior work, they say it depends on parameter count as the complexity measure and is not expected under appropriate regularization or early stopping. They add, again citing prior work, that it generally does not appear in LLM or ViT scaling analyses. Its value, they argue, lies in refining broad theories such as the bias-variance tradeoff, not in narrow ad hoc explanations.
record.recipe_differences: The example tracks prime counts alongside test performance in a setting borrowed from Greydanus & Kobak (2024); it is presented as an intentionally narrow illustrative explanation, not as a reproduction of the original double-descent method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that prime-count tracking is confounded by changing parameter magnitudes; it does not report a systematic sensitivity study.

fits_no_version.finding: The number of prime-valued rounded parameters tracks test performance in the double-descent example (10 seeds, SD shown). The authors attribute this to confounding by growing parameter magnitude and parameter count.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Post hoc parameter statistics (here, prime counts) can track double-descent test curves without test labels, because they are confounded with parameter magnitude and count.

record.peer_reviewed: International Conference on Machine Learning, PMLR 267, 2025
record.problems: The only own result bearing on V1 is a figure without numerical values or detailed experimental specifications. The paper does not state where the peak lies relative to training-set fit. Other claims about practical scaling, regularization, and parameter counting are discussed through cited work rather than tested here.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows. The grokking example concerns a different training-time phenomenon, and cited results on regularization, scaling analyses, and parameter counting are not this paper's own results.

untested.parts: Peak location relative to the training-set interpolation threshold. Any quantitative curve values. Architecture and size range.
All. The grokking panel concerns a different training-time phenomenon.
All. The regularization claim is cited from Nakkiran et al. 2021 and Hastie et al. 2022.
All. The parameter-count caveat is cited from Curth et al. 2024b.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V1 'supports' label are not justified. The double-descent curve is a re-run of a cited setting, used to illustrate an ad hoc hypothesis. The paper's skeptical claims bearing on V6/V7 and on practical relevance are cited, not tested, so no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The relationship between the peak and the size at which the model just fits the training set is not stated.

rows.subject: neural network (Greydanus & Kobak, 2024 setting)
rows.operation_detail: Varied model size in the double-descent example and tracked test performance and the number of prime-valued parameters after rounding.
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation displayed; results averaged over 10 seeds.
rows.locator: Figure 4; Appendix A, Additional Note on Prime Numbers Example
rows.note: The text identifies the left-hand example as double descent and says prime counts accurately track test performance. It does not provide numeric curve values or state the peak's position relative to training-set fit.
rows.check: The test curve is a figure-only reproduction of a borrowed setting, run to illustrate the prime-count metric. No numbers, peak location or interpolation threshold are given, and model sizes and architecture are not specified in the text. The row measures the right quantity, but its value cannot be read and it is not offered as evidence on V1. The label 'observed' cannot be verified from the text.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
